summary: Specifies the QCP file format, which many implementations already used to store QCELP 13K speech and also EVRC and SMV vocoder data. RFC 2658 covered the streaming format but not storage. This document also updates the audio/qcelp media type and registers audio/evrc-qcp and audio/smv-qcp.

plainLanguage.summary: Voice recordings need a box to be saved in. This document describes a box many programs already used, so everyone can save phone voice recordings the same way and open each other's files.

questions: what is the qcp file format
how do i store voice recordings
subtitle: Storage format for speech data from QCELP, EVRC, and SMV vocoders.

tldr.problem: Speech codecs like QCELP 13K, EVRC, and SMV need to be stored in files and exchanged via email and messaging systems, but RFC 2658 only specified how to stream them, not how to store them.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC formalizes the QCP file format, which had been in wide use by software like Eudora and QuickTime to store vocoder data, and registers the audio/qcelp, audio/evrc-qcp and audio/smv-qcp media types.
tldr.outcome: Speech codec data can now be reliably stored and exchanged in a standard format, widely supported by email clients and mobile devices.

facts.label: Magic bytes
facts.value: RIFF at offset 0; QLCM at offset 8

today: RFC 3625 is an Informational RFC describing a widely deployed format. QCP files are commonly used in mobile systems, VoIP applications, and multimedia software to store and exchange speech codec data.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The RFC specifies storage for three speech codecs used in mobile and VoIP systems: QCELP 13K, used in earlier CDMA networks; EVRC, an improved codec; and SMV, a newer codec. RFC 2658 had defined how to stream these codecs over networks, but software implementers—Eudora, QuickTime, and CDMA2000 handsets—had already settled on a common file format, QCP, for storage and email exchange.

This RFC documents the existing QCP format to make it an official standard, so all implementations follow the same rules.
sections.plainLanguage: Phone companies had picked a way to save voice recordings in a file. This RFC wrote down the rules so everyone does it the same way.

sections.title: The QCP File Structure
sections.content:
A QCP file follows the RIFF (Resource Interchange File Format) container, which starts with the magic bytes RIFF followed by a size. The first chunk identifies the file type as QLCM.

The file contains several chunks in order: FMT describes the codec and parameters (codec type, version, bit rate, sample rate, sample size); VRAT marks whether packets are fixed or variable size; optional LABL and OFFS chunks carry labels and time-offset indices; DATA contains the actual codec frames; and optional CNFG and TEXT chunks hold configuration and metadata.

The codec information includes a 16-byte GUID that identifies which codec was used (QCELP, EVRC, or SMV) and its version. For variable-rate codecs, each packet includes a rate octet that determines the packet's length, and a lookup table maps each rate value to the packet size.
sections.plainLanguage: A QCP file is like a labeled box. It says what codec was used, how fast it was recorded, and then stores all the frames in order.

sections.title: Codec Details and Variants
sections.content:
The RFC specifies GUIDs for three codec families: QCELP-13K (two variants), EVRC, and SMV. QCELP frames can be read as variable-rate (each frame's size is in a lookup table) or fixed-rate (all frames the same size).

The FMT chunk stores major and minor version numbers; currently QCELP-13K and EVRC use major version 1 (unchanged for compatibility), while SMV uses major version 2.

The file stores metadata about sampling rate (typically 8000 Hz), sample size in bits (typically 16), average bit rate, and the size of the largest packet. For variable-rate files, a table maps rate octets to packet sizes so decoders can quickly find frame boundaries.
sections.plainLanguage: The file says how many samples per second, how many bits per sample, and a table so you can jump to any part of the voice recording quickly.

sections.title: Media Type Registration
sections.content:
The RFC updates the audio/qcelp media type (originally registered in RFC 2658) to clarify that it is used for file storage, not just streaming. It also updates audio/vnd.qcelp to deprecate it in favor of audio/qcelp.

Two new media types are registered: audio/evrc-qcp for EVRC data and audio/smv-qcp for SMV data, both in the QCP format. The magic number for identification is RIFF at bytes 0-3 and QLCM at bytes 8-11. File extensions are .qcp or .QCP.
sections.plainLanguage: The file gets an official name tag so email programs know it's a voice recording and can play it.

sections.title: Security and Risks
sections.content: The QCP format is a file container only; it does not specify transport or streaming. The security considerations are the same as for any audio codec or media file: a very large file could cause a receiver to run out of memory (denial of service), and security issues with the underlying codecs (QCELP, EVRC, SMV) must be understood before use.
sections.plainLanguage: A huge voice file could freeze someone's phone, and the voice codecs themselves might have issues to watch for.
